To characterize the functional composition of ant and bee communities, we used two widely recognized approaches in ecological research: 1) the community weighted mean (CWM) of traits, which indicates a community's most common traits after accounting for differences in taxon abundance (Laliberté and Legendre, 2010) and 2) the functional diversity (FD) in traits, which indicates how much species within a community vary in their traits (Arnan et al., 2013; Ricotta and Moretti, 2011). CWM and FD values were calculated for each transect.

Given the regional scale of our study, we gathered information on the environmental characteristics of each study area. The resulting set of variables was used as covariables in the analyses (Dataset S1, spreadsheets data.ants and data.bees). This list comprised latitude, longitude, and elevation (Lat, Long, and Elev) as determined from GPS coordinates; lithological types (igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rock) (CSIC-IARA, 1988), as different type of soil affect ant richness and bee nesting for ground-dwelling bees (Angulo et al., 2016; Lybrand et al., 2020; Antoine and Forrest, 2021); pine species (Pine halepensis, P. nigra, P. pinaster, and P. pinea) because pines can differ in their responses to fire (He et al., 2012); and eight bioclimatic variables (WorldClim database v. 2.0— [www.worldclim.org](http://www.worldclim.org); Hijmans et al., 2005). The latter covered the period from 1970 to 2000, and the values had a spatial resolution of about 1 km 2 . Using principal components analysis (PCA), we reduced them to two uncorrelated components that accounted for 92.3 % of the original variation (Clim. 1 and Clim. 2; Table S5).

In preparation for the first GLM, Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated for the response variable and the proportional area of each of the eight land-use types based on the Basis-DLM for each of the twelve radii. For each land-use type, the radius associated with the largest absolute value of correlation coefficient was selected for the first GLM (Table 1, Fig. 2, Online Resource ESM2) to identify the most relevant radius (cf. Steffan-Dewenter et al. 2002). Proportion of land-use types in the selected radii did not show any collinearity (r < 0.7 for all tests). The most appropriate error distribution for the first GLM, which contained the proportional area of the eight land-use types and vegetation characteristics, was chosen according to the findings of Payne et al. (2018). For all response variables, negative binomial error distribution with linear parametrisation was used, except for medium sized bees, where negative binomial error distribution with quadratic parametrisation was used.

text: As a natural boundary between the warm temperate and subtropical zones, the Qinling Mountains, with vast elevational range and remarkably rich biodiversity, provide a unique opportunity to investigate how elevational gradients influence the ant diversity patterns (Hou et al. 2008; Yu et al. 2021). So far, studies conducted in this region have not yet addressed functional and phylogenetic diversity on ants (Wei et al. 2001; He et al. 2003). We performed field research of ant communities in six elevation bands in Ningshan County located in the Qinling Mountains. We tried to determine how the taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic diversity respond to elevations gradients, and analyzed how the functional trait distribution changed at different elevations. We hypothesized that (1) species and functional traits composition of ant communities among different elevations vary, and (2) indices of three aspects diversity decrease with elevations.

As a natural boundary between the warm temperate and subtropical zones, the Qinling Mountains, with vast elevational range and remarkably rich biodiversity, provide a unique opportunity to investigate how elevational gradients influence the ant diversity patterns (Hou et al. 2008; Yu et al. 2021). So far, studies conducted in this region have not yet addressed functional and phylogenetic diversity on ants (Wei et al. 2001; He et al. 2003). We performed field research of ant communities in six elevation bands in Ningshan County located in the Qinling Mountains. We tried to determine how the taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic diversity respond to elevations gradients, and analyzed how the functional trait distribution changed at different elevations. We hypothesized that (1) species and functional traits composition of ant communities among different elevations vary, and (2) indices of three aspects diversity decrease with elevations.

We established six study sites at different elevations, ranging from 967 to 2029 m.a.s.l. The elevational difference between adjacent sites was at least 200 m, and these sites consisted of 1000 (ES1), 1200 (ES2), 1400 (ES3), 1600 (ES4), 1800 (ES5) and 2000 m.a.s.l (ES6) (Table S1). Three plots were designed as replicates in each study site, for a total of 18 sampling plots, referred to as EP1–EP18 (Table S1). The sampling plots were spaced at least 300 m apart.

Multiple comparisons demonstrated that ant species richness, Chao-1, Rao’s Q, FD_PD, PD and MPD at low elevation were significantly higher than those at middle and high elevation, while there was no significant difference in all six indices between middle and high elevation.
